summary: Defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module so SNMP can manage the Baseline Privacy Plus features of DOCSIS 1.1 and 2.0 cable modems and cable modem termination systems. Baseline Privacy Plus covers the security features of cable data service. This is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A cable company needs a control panel to check and adjust the privacy settings of many home cable modems. This memo defines the list of dials and readouts that panel can use.

subtitle: The SNMP objects that let operators monitor and manage the privacy and security features of DOCSIS cable modems.

tldr.problem: Cable operators need a standard way to see and adjust the Baseline Privacy Plus security features of many DOCSIS 1.1 and 2.0 cable modems and their termination systems.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the DOCS-IETF-BPI2-MIB module, a set of SNMP managed objects for key exchange, modem authentication, multicast encryption and authenticated software download.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 9141. Its security section warns that the DES encryption used by BPI+ is weak and that SNMP before SNMPv3 is inadequate.

today: RFC 4131 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9141, and it has not been obsoleted. It defines the BPI+ MIB for DOCSIS 1.1 and 2.0, and its security section recommends SNMPv3.

sections.title: The Management Framework and Purpose
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for network management. Managed objects live in a virtual information store, the MIB, and are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). Objects are written using the Structure of Management Information, and this module follows SMIv2 as described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. For an overview of the framework the memo points to RFC 3410.

The module covers the Baseline Privacy Plus (BPI+) features of DOCSIS 1.1 and DOCSIS 2.0 Cable Modems (CMs) and Cable Modem Termination Systems (CMTSs). It is derived from the operational model in the DOCSIS Baseline Privacy Interface Plus Specification.
sections.eli5: A MIB is a menu of things you can look at or change on a machine from far away. This one is the menu for the privacy features of cable modems.

sections.title: What Baseline Privacy Plus Covers
sections.content:
The memo says BPI+ is made of four distinct functional and manageable areas.

  • Key exchange and data encryption
  • Cable modem authentication
  • Multicast encryption
  • Authentication of downloaded software images

This module extends the DOCSIS 1.0 Baseline Privacy MIB of RFC 3083, and the original structure has mostly been preserved. The text notes that the referenced DOCSIS specifications only require cable modems to process IPv4 customer traffic, and that the design choices reflect this. Future DOCSIS versions are expected to require IPv6 as well.
sections.eli5: The privacy system does four jobs: swap secret keys, check that each modem is genuine, protect group broadcasts, and make sure new software is the real thing. The MIB has dials for all four.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The module sits under docsBpi2MIB, assigned { mib-2 126 }. It is organized as tables and objects, split into cable modem objects, cable modem termination system objects, and common code download objects.

On the cable modem side the tables hold authorization key exchange state (docsBpi2CmBaseTable), traffic key exchange and data encryption per security association (docsBpi2CmTEKTable), IP multicast mappings, device certificates, and the cryptographic suite capabilities of the modem.

On the termination system side they hold default settings and summary counters, authorization key exchange per modem together with data from modem certificates, traffic keys per security association, two multicast tables, and provisioned modem and certification authority certificates. One multicast table is designed specifically for IP multicast encryption; the other manages all multicast security associations.

The IP multicast mask is based on the InetAddress textual convention rather than a prefix length, because it could be a non-contiguous netmask. This lets one security association identifier cover several IPv6 multicast groups across scopes.
sections.eli5: The menu has one page for the modem in your house and another for the big machine at the cable company, plus a shared page for software updates.

sections.title: Textual Conventions and Key Objects
sections.content:
The module defines its own data types. DocsSAId is a Security Association identifier ranging from 1 to 16383; DocsSAIdOrZero also allows zero, meaning the identifier is not yet determined. DocsBpkmSAType names the security association type: primary corresponds to code 1, static to code 2 and dynamic to code 3, with none used only when the type is not yet known. Certificates are carried as DocsX509ASN1DEREncodedCertificate, an X.509 certificate encoded as an ASN.1 DER object of up to 4096 octets.

Per-modem objects report the state of the authorization state machine, the authorization key sequence number (0 to 15), key expiry times, and counters for messages sent and received such as Authorization Request, Reply, Reject and Invalid. Timer values such as the authorization grace time (1 to 6047999 seconds) and the TEK grace time (1 to 302399 seconds) are exposed read-only. The rejected-authorization error code can be unauthorizedCm, unauthorizedSaid, permanentAuthorizationFailure or timeOfDayNotAcquired, among others.

All counters are 32 bits wide, and the Interfaces Group MIB rules of RFC 2863 for counter discontinuities apply.
sections.eli5: Each dial has a type: some show a number in a set range, some show a name like 'primary' or 'dynamic', and some just count how many times something happened.

sections.title: Encryption and Authentication Algorithm Values
sections.content:
The module lists the data encryption algorithms the BPKM cryptographic-suite parameter can name. The value none means the security association has no data encryption.

A separate convention lists data integrity algorithms, where none means no data integrity is used and hmacSha196 is value 1. These are defined for the interface, but the security section says that for BPI+ itself no data integrity mechanism is currently defined.
sections.eli5: The MIB has a list of the lock types a modem could use, from older and weaker ones to newer and stronger ones, and a choice for 'no lock at all'.

sections.title: Authenticated Software Download and Certificates
sections.content:
The common docsBpi2CodeDownloadControl group manages authenticated software download for a device. Its status code reports the result of the latest configuration file CVC verification, SNMP CVC verification or code file verification, with values such as configFileCvcVerified, snmpCvcRejected and codeFileVerified.

Other objects report the manufacturer organization name and access start times, and the co-signer organization name and times. The co-signer name is a zero-length string when no co-signer is specified. Times always refer to GMT and must include time zone information. A read-write object, docsBpi2CodeCvcUpdate, accepts an X.509 certificate.

On the termination system, tables hold provisioned modem certificates and certification authority certificates, which are used to authenticate cable modems.
sections.eli5: Before a modem installs new software, it checks the sender's signed ID card. These objects show whether the check passed or failed, and who signed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Writable objects can be sensitive. Objects that reset authorization or key state, such as docsBpi2CmAuthReset, docsBpi2CmtsAuthCmReset and docsBpi2CmtsTEKReset, start a re-key process, and a massive malicious SET attack may overload the termination system. The key lifetime objects should follow the range constraints in the compliance clause. docsBpi2CmtsDefaultSelfSignedManufCertTrust is designed for testing and is not RECOMMENDED for commercial deployments. Certificate and multicast table objects could be abused to cause denial or theft of service. Readable objects may also reveal which users run without data encryption.

The memo says SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and that deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED; it is RECOMMENDED to use SNMPv3 with cryptographic security.

The BPI+ traffic encryption keys use 40-bit or 56-bit DES in CBC mode, and the memo states that, due to DES weaknesses, future BPI+ revisions should introduce stronger algorithms. Frequent key changes do not necessarily reduce the risk of a DES attack, since the keys can decrypt old traffic. The modem authorization protocol uses triple DES.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can turn these dials could cause trouble, so only trusted people should get access. Also, the lock used on the traffic is old and could be picked.
